title: Varicella (chickenpox) and herpes zoster (India)
specialty: Dermatology / Infectious Diseases / Paediatrics / Primary Care

evidenceAudit.scope: Chickenpox and shingles in adults and children in India: diagnosis, complications and red flags, oral and IV acyclovir, valacyclovir, pain and post-herpetic neuralgia, pregnancy, eye involvement, isolation and referral, built on the ICMR Varicella and Herpes Zoster STW (July 2022).
findings: Clinical diagnosis, optional Tzanck or PCR, complications and red flags, acyclovir 800 mg five times daily for 5–7 days (adults and children over 40 kg) or 20 mg/kg/dose (maximum 800 mg) four times daily for 7 days (under 40 kg), IV acyclovir 10 mg/kg 8-hourly for complicated, haemorrhagic, immunosuppressed or neonatal varicella, valacyclovir 1 g three times daily, zoster treatment within 72 hours for 7 days, pregabalin 150–600 mg/day, gabapentin 300–1800 mg/day, amitriptyline 10–25 mg, nortriptyline 10–75 mg, carbamazepine 200 mg, avoid aspirin, ophthalmicus referral and pregnancy guidance checked against the ICMR Varicella and Herpes Zoster STW (July 2022).

NACI 2016: VarIg 125 IU per 10 kg, maximum 625 IU, ideally within 96 hours and up to 10 days. CDC 2013: IM; minimum 62.5 IU at 2 kg or less and 125 IU at 2.1–10 kg; observe for 28 days; contraindicated after severe reaction to immune globulin or IgA deficiency with anti-IgA antibodies.

UKHSA 2023: oral aciclovir 800 mg four times daily (children 10 mg/kg, maximum 800 mg) or valaciclovir 1 g three times daily (children 20 mg/kg, maximum 1 g) from day 7 to day 14 after exposure is first choice for susceptible pregnant and immunosuppressed contacts; VZIG for neonates exposed within a week of delivery or when antivirals are unsuitable.
unverifiedSections: Isolation duration is not specified in the STW (usually until all lesions crust).

Post-exposure antiviral prophylaxis is from UKHSA (2023) and VarIg details from CDC (2013) and NACI (2016), because the ICMR STW only says VarIg may be considered when vaccination is contraindicated; VarIg may be hard to obtain in India. Renal doses are from the US labels (Drugs.com).
Famciclovir is not mentioned in the STW.
Drug cautions, contraindications and renal or hepatic adjustment lines without a source tag are general pharmacology statements and need formulary confirmation.

pathophysiology.summary: Chickenpox (varicella) is a highly contagious childhood infection that is more severe in adults, pregnant women, newborns and the immunocompromised. Shingles (herpes zoster) is reactivation of the same virus in a dermatome, commonest in older and immunosuppressed people, and its main long-term problem is post-herpetic neuralgia. Diagnosis is clinical. Oral acyclovir started early (within 24 hours of rash for varicella, 72 hours for zoster) shortens illness; IV acyclovir is for complicated disease. Eye involvement (lesions on the forehead or nose tip) needs urgent ophthalmology. Avoid aspirin in children. Susceptible high-risk contacts — pregnant women, newborns and the immunocompromised — need post-exposure immune globulin, and patients remain infectious until all lesions have crusted. Varicella pneumonia, encephalitis and secondary bacterial infection are the main causes of death.
keyMechanisms: Primary infection spreads by droplets and vesicle fluid; incubation 10–21 days.
Virus becomes latent in sensory ganglia; waning immunity allows reactivation as zoster.
Acyclovir inhibits viral DNA polymerase after activation by viral thymidine kinase.

symptoms: Prodrome of fever and headache 1–2 days before the rash (adults)
Eye pain, red eye or blurred vision (zoster ophthalmicus)
physicalSigns: Vesicles on red base in crops at different stages (dew drop on a rose petal) (ICMR STW)
Grouped vesicles in one dermatome (ICMR STW)
Lesions on forehead or nose tip (ophthalmicus) (ICMR STW)
Facial palsy with vesicles in the ear canal (Ramsay Hunt syndrome)
redFlags: Haemorrhagic or necrotic lesions; multi-dermatomal or disseminated zoster (ICMR STW)
precipitants: Pregnancy, newborn of a mother with peripartum varicella, no prior chickenpox or vaccination

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Small oval vesicles on palms, soles and mouth in young children, not in crops on the trunk; clinical diagnosis.
Honey-coloured crusts around nose and mouth without crops of vesicles; Gram stain or culture settles it.
Grouped vesicles that recur at the same site, not following a dermatome; viral PCR of a vesicle settles it.
Itchy papules with a central punctum on exposed skin, no fever or crops; history settles it.
Recurrent, multidermatomal or severe zoster in a young adult; HIV testing settles it (general practice).
Deep lesions all at the same stage, often on palms, soles or genitals, with tender lymph nodes; PCR of lesion fluid settles it.

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Fever with generalised vesicles in different stages.
Grouped vesicles in a dermatome with pain.
Systemic complications, haemorrhagic varicella, immunosuppression, neonatal varicella, disseminated zoster.

clinicalManagement.title: Assess
actions: Look for red flags, pregnancy, immunosuppression and eye involvement (ICMR STW).
Ask about high-risk contacts at home (pregnant, newborn, immunosuppressed) who may need VarIg (NACI).

clinicalManagement.title: Varicella
actions: Oral acyclovir within 24 hours of rash for infants, children over 12, adults, pregnant women and the immunosuppressed; IV acyclovir for complications (ICMR STW). Healthy children aged 1–12 get symptomatic care.
Paracetamol for fever; antihistamine; daily bath; avoid aspirin (ICMR STW).
Pregnancy: treat with acyclovir and refer; infection in the first 20 weeks may cause congenital varicella syndrome, and perinatal maternal varicella may cause neonatal varicella (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Herpes zoster
actions: Acyclovir or valacyclovir for 7 days; later if new lesions, ophthalmicus or Ramsay Hunt (ICMR STW).
NSAIDs for pain; add pregabalin, gabapentin or a tricyclic if uncontrolled (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Protect exposed contacts
actions: Susceptible pregnant or immunosuppressed contacts: oral aciclovir 800 mg four times daily (or valaciclovir 1 g three times daily) from day 7 to day 14 after exposure (UKHSA).
Neonates exposed within a week of delivery, or when antivirals are unsuitable: VarIg 125 IU per 10 kg IM, maximum 625 IU, as soon as possible and within 10 days; observe for 28 days (NACI; CDC).
Prevention: live varicella vaccine at 12–15 months and 4–6 years, 2 doses for those 13 and over; zoster vaccine may be offered over 50 years (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Refer
actions: Eye involvement: ophthalmology; ear lesions or facial weakness (Ramsay Hunt): ENT (ICMR STW).
Complications, immunosuppression, haemorrhagic varicella, failure of oral acyclovir, neonatal varicella, multidermatomal or disseminated zoster, post-herpetic neuralgia (ICMR STW).

vignette.text: Mrs S, a 26-year-old schoolteacher from Pune who is 20 weeks pregnant, phones because her 5-year-old son developed an itchy blistering rash yesterday. She does not remember having chickenpox and has not been vaccinated. She feels well. Her son has fever and crops of vesicles on his trunk, with new crops still appearing. Her elderly father, who lives with them, is on chemotherapy for lymphoma.

guidedApproach.title: Primary infection, latency and reactivation
guidedApproach.prompt: Why does the same virus cause two diseases?
guidedApproach.guidance: Varicella zoster virus enters through the respiratory tract, replicates in lymphoid tissue and spreads in the blood to the skin, producing crops of vesicles at different stages. It is infectious from about 2 days before the rash until all lesions crust. The virus then becomes latent in sensory ganglia. When cell-mediated immunity falls — with age, HIV, cancer or steroids — it reactivates and travels down one sensory nerve, causing dermatomal pain followed by vesicles (zoster). Nerve inflammation explains post-herpetic neuralgia. Severe disease in adults, pregnancy and immunosuppression reflects the importance of T-cell immunity in controlling the virus.

guidedApproach.title: Spot the complications early
guidedApproach.guidance: In varicella, look for breathlessness or chest pain (pneumonia, especially in adults, smokers and pregnant women), confusion or ataxia (encephalitis, cerebellitis), haemorrhagic lesions and secondary bacterial infection. In zoster, lesions on the forehead, nose tip or eye suggest ophthalmic involvement (Hutchinson's sign) and need urgent ophthalmology; facial palsy with ear vesicles is Ramsay Hunt syndrome. Zoster in more than one dermatome, dissemination, or recurrent zoster in a young adult should prompt HIV testing. Ask every patient about pregnant, newborn and immunosuppressed contacts.

guidedApproach.title: Clinical diagnosis, tests for doubt
guidedApproach.guidance: Most varicella and zoster are diagnosed clinically. Testing is useful when the rash is atypical, in immunosuppressed patients, or in pregnancy: vesicle fluid PCR is the most sensitive test. Varicella IgG serology confirms immunity in an exposed pregnant woman or immunocompromised contact with uncertain history, but should not delay VarIg beyond the window. A chest X-ray assesses suspected pneumonia, and lumbar puncture suspected encephalitis. HIV testing is advised in recurrent or severe zoster. Renal function guides acyclovir dosing in older adults and those receiving IV treatment.

guidedApproach.title: Antivirals, analgesia and protecting contacts
guidedApproach.prompt: How do you treat and protect?
guidedApproach.guidance: Start oral acyclovir 800 mg five times daily for 5–7 days in adults, adolescents, pregnant women and the immunosuppressed within 24 hours of varicella rash (children under 40 kg 20 mg/kg four times daily, maximum 800 mg). For zoster, acyclovir 800 mg five times daily or valacyclovir 1 g three times daily for 7 days, ideally within 72 hours, or later if new lesions or eye involvement. Complicated or immunosuppressed patients need IV acyclovir 10 mg/kg every 8 hours with hydration. Treat pain with an NSAID and add pregabalin, gabapentin or amitriptyline for neuropathic pain. Avoid aspirin in children. Susceptible pregnant or immunosuppressed contacts receive oral aciclovir or valaciclovir from day 7 to 14 after exposure, and exposed newborns VarIg 125 IU per 10 kg IM.

boardQuestions.vignette: A 26-year-old woman who is 20 weeks pregnant was exposed yesterday to her son's chickenpox at home. She has no history of chickenpox or vaccination, is well, and her varicella IgG is negative. Her kidney function is normal and she has no other illness. She asks whether she needs any treatment.
boardQuestions.question: What is the most appropriate management?

options.explanation: Live vaccines are contraindicated in pregnancy, so this is unsafe.

options.text: Reassure; treat only if a rash develops
options.explanation: A susceptible pregnant woman is high risk and should be offered prophylaxis (UKHSA).

options.text: Oral aciclovir 800 mg five times daily starting today for 7 days
options.explanation: Prophylactic antivirals are given from day 7 to day 14 after exposure, not straight away (UKHSA).

options.text: Oral aciclovir 800 mg four times daily from day 7 to day 14 after exposure
options.explanation: Correct. Antivirals are now first choice for susceptible pregnant contacts; VarIg is for those who cannot take them (UKHSA).
Exposure alone is not an indication; congenital varicella risk is low.

boardQuestions.keyPoint: Susceptible pregnant contact: oral antiviral from day 7 to 14; VarIg if antivirals unsuitable.

boardQuestions.vignette: A 68-year-old man has had burning pain over his right forehead for 3 days and now has vesicles on the forehead and the tip of his nose. His right eye is red and watering. He has diabetes and creatinine is normal.
boardQuestions.question: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Oral acyclovir 800 mg five times daily and urgent ophthalmology review
options.explanation: Correct. Nose-tip lesions suggest ophthalmic involvement, so antiviral treatment and urgent eye review are needed (ICMR STW).
Topical treatment does not prevent eye complications from zoster ophthalmicus.
Analgesia is needed but does not treat the virus or protect the eye.

options.text: Give an antiviral only if new lesions appear
options.explanation: Eye involvement needs antiviral treatment now, whether or not new lesions appear (ICMR STW).
Steroids alone without antivirals are not recommended in zoster.

boardQuestions.keyPoint: Nose-tip vesicles: think eye involvement and refer urgently.

boardQuestions.vignette: A 30-year-old man has had chickenpox for 3 days. Today he is breathless, with SpO2 89% on air, respiratory rate 30/min and bilateral crackles. Chest X-ray shows diffuse nodular shadows. He smokes 15 cigarettes a day and weighs 70 kg.
boardQuestions.question: What is the best treatment?

options.text: Oral acyclovir 800 mg five times daily at home
options.explanation: Pneumonia is a complication needing admission and IV treatment.

options.text: Oral valacyclovir 1 g three times daily
options.explanation: Oral treatment is inadequate for life-threatening varicella pneumonia.

options.text: Admit; IV acyclovir 10 mg/kg (700 mg) every 8 hours with oxygen
options.explanation: Correct. Varicella pneumonia needs IV acyclovir 10 mg/kg every 8 hours and supportive care (ICMR STW).
VarIg is prophylaxis for exposed contacts, not treatment of established disease.
Aspirin is avoided in varicella and fluids alone do not treat the infection.

boardQuestions.educationalObjective: Treat complicated varicella with IV acyclovir.
boardQuestions.keyPoint: Varicella pneumonia: admit and give IV acyclovir.

patientEducation: Stay away from pregnant women, newborns and immunocompromised people until lesions crust.
Do not scratch; keep nails short.
lifestyleAndDiet: Fluids; soft diet if mouth ulcers.
dischargeCriteria: Afebrile, no complications, oral treatment tolerated
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Review in 3–5 days for complications; pain review for zoster at 2–4 weeks.
